title: Break up prolonged sitting
content: Sitting for long periods without interruption is linked to poorer health. Standing up, changing position or moving for a few minutes at regular intervals (for example every 30-60 minutes) is a common recommendation for desk workers.

title: Short walking breaks
content: Adults are encouraged to limit sedentary time and replace it with physical activity of any intensity. A brief walk to refill water, use the stairs or talk to a colleague in person is an easy way to add movement.

title: Seated posture basics
content: Sit with feet supported on the floor or a footrest, knees roughly level with the hips, and the lower back supported by the chair backrest. Avoid sitting in the same fixed posture for a long time; small posture changes help.

title: Monitor height and distance
content: Place the top of the screen at or slightly below eye level and about an arm's length away, directly in front of you. A screen that is too high or too low or off to one side encourages neck and shoulder strain.

title: Keyboard and mouse position
content: Keep the keyboard and mouse close to the body so the elbows stay near the sides and bent at about 90 degrees, with wrists in a neutral, straight position rather than bent up or sideways.

title: 20-20-20 rule for eye strain
content: To reduce digital eye strain, every 20 minutes look at something about 20 feet (6 metres) away for at least 20 seconds. Blinking fully and adjusting screen brightness to match the room can also help.
source_name: American Optometric Association - Computer vision syndrome

title: Gentle neck and shoulder stretches
content: Slow, gentle stretches such as tilting the ear toward the shoulder or rolling the shoulders back can ease stiffness from desk work. Stretch only to mild tension, hold briefly, breathe normally, and stop if there is pain.

title: Staying active with lower back discomfort
content: For mild back pain, staying active and continuing normal activities as far as possible is usually better than prolonged rest. Gentle movement and stretching can help; seek medical advice if pain is severe or does not improve.

title: Rest and stretch hands and wrists
content: During long periods of typing or mouse use, take short pauses and gently open and stretch the fingers and wrists. Avoid resting the wrists on hard edges while typing.

title: Microbreaks reduce strain
content: Brief, frequent breaks from computer tasks (a minute or two, taken often) are recommended to relieve muscle tension and visual fatigue, and are generally easier to keep up than a few long breaks.

title: Breathing exercise for stress and tension
content: A simple breathing exercise - breathing in slowly through the nose and out through the mouth for a few minutes while sitting comfortably - can help people feel calmer when stressed or tense.

title: Tiredness and daily habits
content: Everyday tiredness is often helped by regular sleep times, some daily physical activity, drinking enough water and a manageable workload. Persistent unexplained tiredness should be discussed with a doctor.
